utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. Laurie Sartorio and Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson representing General Rasim Delic, with Lejla Gluhic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir. Could you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My colleague, Ms. Sartorio, will be taking this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your full name, and give us your current occupation and the city and country in which you live.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Fadil Imamovic. I'm a civil servant right now. I live in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, in 1993 to 1995, did you hold any positions in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And if so, would you please tell the Chamber about those positions and the time period in which you served?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Between 1993 and 1995, or rather 1996, I held various posts in the BH Army. I was the commander of the 311th Light Brigade until October 1994, and then I was the assistant commander for Security in the 35th Division of the BH Army, first in the Bosna Operations Group, which was the predecessor of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long were you in that post?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander for Security in the 35th Division from October 1994 until mid-September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'd like to focus --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Sartorio please switch off the microphone while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please switch off the microphone while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Every time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That looks like that's the request.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll just lean over the podium, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to focus your attention right now on your position as assistant commander for Security in the 35th Division in the summer of 1995. Before that, though, could you please tell us what the function or purpose was of the security division -- of the 35th Division, or was it called the Security Department, or what was the name of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue of your switching on and off your mic is recurrent, because when somebody next to you is typing, the noise is terrible, and even for us as we listen to it, so I don't know how that can be resolved. Maybe your case manager or the senior trial attorney can move to the other table or somehow -- I don't know how to solve it, but that's the problem. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining that, Your Honour, and I will do it and we'll see how it goes, and then I'll ask my senior trial attorney to move if it's a problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, sir? I asked you to tell us what the function or purpose was of the Security division or department of the 35th Division. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the Security Department in the 35th Division was the same as in other commands of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, taking various measures to ensure the security of the commands and units in the field and at command posts, coordinating the work of the military police. It was, in fact, a technical organ of the commander that dealt with security-related issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us how the Security Department of the 35th Division was organised and also if there where security departments or organs of other battalions and brigades, how they are organised and how it all works, please?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 35th Division had his assistant for Security, who set up the department, with four of his associates, officers. In the brigade commands, the commander again had his assistant for Security. They had two or three associates. At the battalion level, there was also the assistant commander for Security, and he would have one or two associates, depending on the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, on a daily basis, I'd like you to tell us what your regular duties might be and also the interaction that you had with the other assistant commanders for Security at the battalion and brigade levels.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: My daily duties began with the morning briefing to the commander, but that was not every morning. And then during the day, we'd process the information that had come in, and we'd submit this information to our superiors, or we would visit the battalion commands, the brigade commands to exchange information with the assistant commanders there or officers who worked in that area, that sphere. We'd also coordinate and provide technical assistance to the military police operating there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned during the day you would process information that had come in. Can you tell us, what were the sources of the information that the security organ received in order to process the information?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the sources of information varied. Information came from the field. We gathered information ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So your associates would go out and actually gather intelligence information, or did you work in conjunction with the Intelligence Department?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some information was received from the intelligence organ. We exchanged information with them, anything that was of interest to us that had to do with security measures to be implemented in the units, since the intelligence organ gathered information about the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you in a few minutes about the specifics about the reporting procedures and exactly how reports were made and where they were sent, but first I'd like you to just give us an example of what might be a security issue that you would receive information about, and then explain what you would do -- what the next step you would take after receiving that information.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just to give you an example, if we received information that there is a large number of people who were absent without any justification in a unit, we'd get this kind of information from the security organ in the battalion or the brigade. Again, everything would go through the Security Service channels. We would then process this information in the Security Service at the 35th Division level, and then this information would be relayed to the commander of the 35th Division. And then again the security organ in the 3rd Corps would be also informed about that. That was along the technical channels, so these were our responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then once reports went up to the 35th Division commander, and just for the record, could you identify who that was during the summer of 1995 when you were the assistant commander for Security?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 35th Division was Colonel Fadil Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you also, for the record, tell us who your co-part was or who was the assistant commander for Security in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: In the period when I became the assistant commander for Security, the assistant commander for Security in the 3rd Corps was Ramiz Dugalic. He was succeeded by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the second name?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: And then in the summer or rather in September, it was Agan Haseljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And again we'll get to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Are you going to ask -- the interpreters asked that the witness be asked to repeat the second name of the first person. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat the second name of the first person that you talked about, the assistant commander for Security in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Ramiz Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, it's the second person who was named.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, the first person I see is "Fadil Hasanagic" and then "Ramiz Dugalic," and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, it's the second assistant commander, the one who took over from Ramiz Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, who took over for Ramiz Dugalic again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just start all over again, because all these names are confused. Just start all over again on the names. Link the name to the position and the division or the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In terms of the 35th Division, would you please repeat and slowly say the names so they can take it down in the transcript, the commander of the 35th Division in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Fadil Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in the 3rd Corps, who was the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in the 3rd Corps, in the Security Department or organ of the 3rd Corps, who was the assistant commander of that organ?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, the assistant commander was Ekrem Alihodzic. He was succeeded in late summer by Agan Haseljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you also work in conjunction -- I believe you mentioned earlier that you did have some relationship with the military police units. Can you explain how that relationship or interaction worked?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: The security organ had, as one of its responsibilities, to coordinate and direct the work of the military police in technical terms, but it had no right to decide how to deploy the military police. So to train, to assist in the training of the military police, and in the performance of its day-to-day duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But if there was a security issue in the field, would you work together with the military police to solve the security problem?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you about reports. When you received information on, say, a particular day, did you prepare a report? And if so, tell us the path that the report would take after you prepared it.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: All the events of any interest were put in a report that was prepared by the security organ, and then this report was sent over a special channel of communication to the security organ in the 3rd Corps. Now, as for all important events, events of any interest, we informed the commander of the 35th Division of all that in order to facilitate his decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you also send a copy of the report to the commander of the 35th Division, in addition to sending it to the security organ of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: From time to time. Mostly it was just an informative report, but the commander of the 35th Division was informed through regular briefings or in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us what would constitute, in your opinion, events of interest, as you put it at line 21?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, any events that created the disturbance in the normal life or work of the units in the field; desertion, violations of military discipline, if a crime was committed or a disciplinary infraction, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would opposition soldiers being taken captive or being taken as prisoners of war be one of those important events that you would report?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the actual physical submission of reports, how was that done? Did you use a certain system, a packet system, or any other type of system? Could you please tell the Judges how reports were transmitted?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: The reports that were sent up the technical chain to the security organ in the 3rd Corps were sent using encrypted packet radio, or we sometimes sent it by courier, depending on our actual capabilities. But in most cases, we used packet communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you experience any transmission problems to the extent that you felt that it was becoming to a point that you couldn't relay your reports?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, given the circumstances, it was wartime, sometimes it was difficult to submit the reports, communications would be down, and we would then have to send a courier. So there were those extraordinary circumstances from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. May the witness be shown P02110.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this document in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report about the combat operations that were carried out. It contains the information from the operations report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is this one of your -- considered one of your regular daily reports that you submitted?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it might be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could the witness -- well, there's only one page in the B/C/S -- the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, is that your name at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So is it likely that this was one of your reports, if your name is at the end of it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And back to the first page in English. Would you look at the date? I believe it appears to be a typo to me, but could you tell me what the date is? It says: "May 27th, 2995". Is that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, That's what my translation shows in English, Your Honour, but I -- I'm sorry, excuse me, I'm sorry. That's my -- up top. I'm sorry. It is 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you agree with me the date is the 27th of May, 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I assume it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this report appears to be going to the 3rd Corps Security Service Department?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, sir, would you know where the source of the information for this report was obtained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you know where the source of the information for this report was obtained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was obtained? The source was obtained or the information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The information that's contained in the report, does he know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Does he --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- know what the source of this information was, full stop. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. Could Madam Prosecutor first establish what kind of information we're talking about, what section of the document, and then go on and ask further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, could we turn to the second page in English again, and it's only one page in B/C/S, and I would ask the witness to look at the last paragraph, please, starting with: "The Chetniks ..." and it discusses -- the last sentence says: "32 of them are from the El Mudjahid Detachment." I'm trying to asking you if this is one of your reports, which it purports to be since your name is at the end, where would you -- where would the information have come from that you put into this report? Were there logbooks, were there other matters kept at the subunits?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that this report was drafted by one of my associates and that he obtained this information through the exchange of information with the operations organ, because this contains mostly information from the operations organ or officers -- officer from the 35th Division. Since there are no events that are relevant for security, except for the number of wounded and -- well, except for the number of wounded, that would be the only piece of information that would be of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution requests that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 574.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Sartorio, I would like to take this opportunity to tell you that you have to speak a bit more slowly and wait for the interpreters to finish interpreting everything that is being said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. May the witness be shown P02414.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could we show the witness the second page so he may see it, and also for the English version so that the Court -- it's the third page of the document in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, this is not your signature on the last page, is it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But it has your name typed; correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was probably signed by one of my associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And would that be signed on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at -- under section 3 of this document, which is page 2 of the English. It's number 3. And tell us what that -- it's titled "Situations in the Commands, Units and Institutions of the Army." At the end of that paragraph, it discusses training, joint training between the El Mudjahedin Detachment and the 328th Mountain Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And it also mentions psychological training. Could you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the kind of training that mostly boiled down to religious education and measures to build trust between the members of the El Mudjahid Detachment and the 328th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: From whom would an order come that would permit or order joint training? Where would that order have to come from?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any such order, but I assume that it would have had to come from the commander of the 35th Division, but I cannot claim that or confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, if you look on the first page of the document, back to the first page, it mentions daily report, and it says: "We are forwarding the daily report on security-relevant events and information in the 35th Division area of responsibility." So this would be an example of one of your daily reports; is that -- is that what this is?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 575.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, in addition to daily reports, did you also submit other types of reports, special reports, if certain events occurred?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if there were any events that warranted such urgent interim reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness now be shown P02088. And if we may go to the second page in English so we may see the signature, please. There's no signature, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But on the Bosnian document, sir, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So if you go back to the first page in English, please, is this an example of one of the interim reports that you would send, in addition to your daily reports?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is not a report. It is a cover letter accompanying physical evidence about an event that had security implications.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the substance of this letter, would you please tell the Judges what the substance of this letter was?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a cover letter for the video-recordings of the desecration of the Orthodox cemetery in the village of Curici in the Zavidovici Municipality. The cemetery was desecrated by members of the El Mujahedin unit. So we have the recordings, the official records made by the security organs who were actually there on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know or are you aware or did you hear whether anything -- any response was made to this letter and the attaching documents? In other words, was an investigation conducted?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm that, but it is possible that somebody may have been prosecuted for this. But I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If there was an order that came down for some type of action to be taken, would you have been notified -- would your organ have been notified of this?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, you never received a response to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. This is extremely leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, did you ever receive a response to this letter with the attaching information?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we ask this document be admitted in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 576.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to now be shown P02370. And if we may go to the last page of the document so that we can see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, is this another document that appears to have come from you to the 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you explain briefly to the Court what the substance was of the discussion about -- within the document, in terms of movement of members of the 328th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to that discussion, Madam Sartorio, I just want to get clarification here. I'm looking at the last page of both the B/C/S and the English. The witness's signature is not there, and below his name it's stated that the document is certified by signature and stamp. I'd like to be shown the signature and the stamp, please. Can you see them? Can you see your signature on the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see any stamp of your office on that? Can we please have that last page of the B/C/S. Is there any stamp there from your office, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you read the words in brackets -- the words below your name, please, and tell us what they say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Certified by signature and stamp."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, why would that be written there if both your signature and stamp are not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this was submitted to the 3rd Corps Security Department via packet communications on the basis of the original document that had a stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did the original document have your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had that not been the case, this would never have been submitted to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you telling us that this is a copy and not the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a copy that was sent by packet communications, but that sort of channel was not appropriate for sending through any signatures or stamps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand that answer. Can you clarify what you mean by that? Why would the channel of communication not be appropriate for sending documents that are signed and stamped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that the document we're looking at has an original where, indeed, one does find both a stamp and a signature. Whichever operator was operating this particular piece of equipment at the time was unable to send this document through without the original. That's what the rules were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, we need to go to the first page of the English and also the B/C/S and ask you to -- the first paragraph of the document describes what the subject matter of the document is, and is the subject matter of this document the fact that soldiers from the 328th Brigade have, on their own, transferred over to another unit?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What does this document then -- what is the subject matter of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, it would be helpful if you could ask questions rather than tell the witness, because are you saying to him, "Is the document talking about transfer of members of the 328th Mountain Brigade on their own to another unit?" I don't see that on the English. I see the sentence ends at "and," and I don't know, "and" what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I need to read the beginning of the document up to the section: "Fourth Mountain Battalion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but had you the first page visible to the witness, and the witness can only answer you on what he sees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. It is on the first page in the B/C/S copy, Your Honour. But in the English copy, it starts at the bottom of the first page and runs into the second page, up to the fourth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And so I wanted him to read that and explain what that is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please don't do that. Ask him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, could you please explain what that first paragraph, up to that "4th Manoeuvre Battalion," is about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have from the beginning of the English up to the 4th? We have the last paragraph before the "4th Manoeuvre Battalion."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We need to go to page 1 in English so the Judges can read the first sentence, and then please transfer it over to the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My question is: What is the subject matter of this paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that we are informing the 3rd Corps Command about through the Security Service. We are telling them that since the 26th of July, 1995, several soldiers had willfully abandoned their units, several BH Army soldiers, and joined the El Mudjahid Detachment. Therefore, this is a case of soldiers leaving one unit and joining another outside the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What do you mean by "outside the regular procedure"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the document states, this is willful abandonment of units, no prior approval from appropriate officers, no signed documents signed "Order" telling them to actually do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm asking you because this, of course, is essential to our understanding of this case, because I wanted to be sure that what you were referring to was the way in which these soldiers deserted from one -- transferred themselves from one unit to another, because the other alternative could have been to say that the El Mujahid Detachment was outside the sphere of the ABiH. But I'm sure we will come to that at a later stage. But you have explained what you meant, and I'm grateful for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, this security report was sent to the 3rd Corps Military Security Service Department, as well as to the 35th Division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was addressed to the 3rd Corps Command Military Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And was there any response that you received, to your knowledge, to this concern?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't quite remember, but I do think there was an order telling the commanders to bring those soldiers back to their units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Sartorio, I'm so sorry to interrupt you. However, there is something that I would like to find out before we move on to a different document. What about the B/C/S version of this document? Is the word "desertion" actually used, as in "the soldiers deserted," or what does it say exactly, that they merely transferred to another unit of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the only phrase I can see being used here is "leaving their unit of their own will, without authorisation," and that's all I can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask that the witness be shown P02370.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What we have just seen?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Sorry, Your Honours. P02431. That was admitted as Exhibit 401 -- P02431.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, this is quite a lengthy document, but, sir, are you able to identify this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the description of a situation that we referred to as "combat readiness" throughout unit commands of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And may we go to the last page of the document to see the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, is that your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown -- it's page 11 in the B/C/S version and page 19 in English. Just one moment, Your Honour. Actually, if we look on page 11 of the English, and it's the bottom of the page, and we're going to move from 11 to 12. But in B/C/S, it is on page 7, and it's under section 10, which is titled "The 328th Mountain Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So we see the English -- the bottom is only "328th Mountain Brigade," so we need to go to the next page. And, actually, the bottom of -- sorry, Your Honours. The last word on page 12 of the English, and then go over to 13. That's what I would like the Judges to see. And in the B/C/S, it is in the middle of the page on page 7, and it's discussing the El Mudjahedin Detachment. Has the witness found that section of the document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the English be turned over so that we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could we just discuss this one paragraph for a few minutes and break it down? In what way did the El Mudjahedin Detachment have a positive influence on the combat morale of the 328th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: It's a well-known fact that members of the El Mujahid Detachment were exceptionally brave. The BH Army soldiers derived a lot of self-confidence, morale and courage from their presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then you talk about the negative effects. Could you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The counter-effect or negative effect, if you like, of their presence and any joint actions with the BH Army was this: They, members of the El Mujahid Detachment, tried, in any which way they could, to impose their way of life, their religious practices, certain customs and ways. That did not sit well with the mentality prevailing among the locals. One example of this would be the way they treated women, the way they dressed, the way they practiced religion. Among other things, the way they bathed in the nearby river, this sometimes led to incidents. The locals were, in fact, themselves members of the 328th Brigade, their families, their wives, daughters, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Were they also members of the 328th Brigade, their families, their wives, their daughters and sons and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was really trying to say is that members of the El Mujahid Detachment treated their families like that, out in the street, in the middle of the village, that sort of thing, while their brothers, fathers, and parents were somewhere at the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand this answer. Members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, they treat their families while their fathers are in the front line. I would imagine that these members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment would also be in the front line, so there would be nobody to treat their families otherwise back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about situations from everyday life, things that happened in the town. For example, a member of the El Mujahid Detachment sees girls swimming in the river, he's likely to do something about this, to drive them away, to act in an aggressive manner, that sort of thing. Alternatively, for example, he saw someone smoking or drinking alcohol, they had a strict ban on those things, and sometimes when facing situations of that kind, they could get aggressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's a much more clearer answer to the question than anything else. Thank you very much. Madam Sartorio, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 578.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who the El Mujahid Detachment was subordinated to, what unit, if any?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I have seen a number of documents, and those have led me to believe that it was the Command of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you've seen some documents today, and we're going to see more documents, where you did report on the El Mujahid Detachment; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So what is the reason for you reporting on them -- I'll withdraw that question, Your Honour. May the witness be shown P02441. Sir, I'd like you to first, and also the Judges, look at the top of the document, and then we'll go to the signature page. Sir, this document is dated the 24th of August, 1995, and it's coming from the assistant commander for Security to the 35th Division Military Police Company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now could we go to the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a routine document telling the military police to take certain security measures in the area, monitoring all movement in the area, setting up certain check-points, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'd like to direct the witness's attention to the second page of the B/C/S, starting with the initials "SVI," and page 3 of English, which is close to the bottom of the page, where it discusses all prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Has the witness found the section of the document "SVI"?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what this paragraph specifically refers to?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This part about POWs talks about procedure, the procedure of taking POWs and keeping them, should any be captured in the midst of combat operations. So this is about the relevant procedures, and it says how these POWs were to be treated. It also talks about deserters, about war booty, and about reporting, the reporting system. It's mainly about the procedural aspects of all these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And could you please explain those abbreviations in that paragraph, "VP" to "OBO," "OB"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "VP" means military police, "OBO" is the intelligence organ, and "OB" stands for security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what the relevant procedures would be, in terms of what to do when POWs are captured? Let me rephrase that. When members of the opposing army are captured and become prisoners of war, what were the procedures that were to be followed, according to your department?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever an enemy soldier was captured, this soldier would be handed over immediately to the military police. They were then taken to the Military Police Company HQ in Zavidovici. There would normally be a brief interview, and this captured person would be sent along to Zenica. In addition to all of this, one was always adamant about the strictest possible compliance with the Geneva Conventions and what they say about the treatment of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So were there certain procedures in place, in terms of notification that prisoners had been taken into custody, and then someone was to transport them? Were those procedures in place?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, a POW would be taken from the front to the military police HQ. The military police -- the military police commander in Zenica, the Military police Battalion commander in Zenica would then be informed, and he would then take measures for these POWs to be taken to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in the summer of 1995, were you aware of any prisoners of war or any members of the VRS or other opposing armies being taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean July 2005? Yes. 1995, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, 1995, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how did you receive notification, and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I personally met the first POWs in Livade village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And tell us how -- walk us through how you became aware of these POWs, and what you did, and whether you saw them, from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the vicinity of Livade village. I can't even remember why I happened to be in the area. I found out by chance from a soldier that I had bumped into that there were some POWs in a nearby house. I went to that house and found an armed guard standing outside the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you go there alone, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as far as I remember, I was alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us anything about this armed guard standing outside the house, if he was part of what unit or ...?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: There was just a single armed guard standing there. Judging by his looks, his clothes, with no BH Army insignia displayed, I deduced that this was a member of the El Mujahid Detachment. I tried to talk to him for him to allow me into the house so that I could see the prisoners. He had a radio device, and he spoke in a mixture of Bosnian and another foreign language. He used the device to ask someone's permission to let me in. To my great surprise, he okayed this, he said that I could go in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know who he phoned, did you hear a name, or who he contacted on the radio.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This was a mixture of Bosnian and another foreign language. I did seem to catch the name "Abu Maali" at one time or another, but I can't be positive about this. This was a small house, just ground floor, a village house, which I entered followed by this guard. I was under a lot of pressure. This was the first time that I was coming into contact with POWs. Throughout this time, I had an armed and ostensibly nervous guard standing right behind me. When I walked into a small room, in one of the corners I saw a large group of soldiers seated on the floor. In another corner, there was a smaller group. Because of my mood, because of my state, I couldn't really see whether their hands were tied. All of them -- some of them -- were there any restraints on all of them, any of them, and what sort of restraints exactly. They were all seated on the floor, all quite closely together, and they were obviously very, very scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a good time to take a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed it is, if it is convenient to you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: One point. I'm sorry. I forgot to ask that the previous document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour, P02441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P02441 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court will adjourn and come back at quarter after 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we were discussing you were in a house in Livade and you saw some groups of prisoners sitting on the floor in this house. Can you describe again the layout of the house and how many prisoners that you saw, and if they were in different groups, how many in each group?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a small single-storey village house. There was a corridor, and I think there were two small rooms. And in one of those two small rooms, when I got in there, I saw a large group of prisoners in one corner and a smaller group of prisoners in another corner. They were all sitting on the floor, and I was able to learn from this larger group of prisoners -- or rather they told me that they were Muslims, Bosniaks, who had served in the Republika Srpska Army as a work platoon. They said there were 11 of them. And opposite them, in the other corner, there were three soldiers, if I remember correctly, of the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, once you entered the house, were you able to talk to any of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely what I wanted to do, but the situation was very tense, and when those prisoners from the larger group told me who they were, I went to speak to the smaller group, and I asked them as quickly as I could to tell me their names and what units they were in. They told me that, but I actually wanted to ask them about how they were captured. But another armed soldier appeared just then, and he started yelling at me, and he motioned to me to get out, using hand gestures. He spoke a language I couldn't understand, but what I could understand, on the basis of his hand gestures and his aggressive attitude, that it would be better for me to get out, for reasons of my personal safety. All this happened very quickly, so I wasn't able to observe all that much, apart from what I was able to jot down in that brief conversation where I tried to get their personal details, their full names and the unit they belonged to. This was a very bad situation, and I was very much affected by it as I went back to my office in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you went back to your office in Zavidovici, what did you do? Did you report this to someone, and to whom?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This brief note that I made, I probably gave to my associates, and at the end of the day they drafted a comprehensive report that included other events, and this was sent to the security organ in the 35th Division or, rather, the security organ in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would like the witness, please, to be shown Exhibit 553, which is on my exhibit list to the Defence. It was P02288 at the time I submitted my exhibit list, and it's one page in the B/C/S and it's three pages in English. Could we see the first page in English, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, is this -- well, and also could we see the bottom of the B/C/S and also, for the Judges, page 2 of English. And, sir, is that your name at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could we -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, while we are finding the right page, could you just clarify one little thing for me? Maybe you have already told so, but I might have forgotten. First of all, which day was this; do you remember? And, secondly, were you alone when you went to see these two groups of prisoners? Were you escorted by anybody else than by the Mujahid guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was this date, the 22nd of July. This is when I made this note, and the note itself indicates that the intelligence organ was present there. But I really can't recall anyone being there with me, so I can't really confirm whether this person was there with me because I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can we enlarge the bottom of the document to see if the witness is able to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In the lower right-hand corner, sir, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a poor copy, but from what I can see, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of the English, and there's the section that starts: "Until 1300 hours ..." If you could find that, sir, on your copy, the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could we enlarge his copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you see "1300", the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if you read that paragraph, is this the substance of the report that you submitted to your associates that ultimately went into this report?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how my associates who drafted this came to be in possession of this information. Probably in cooperation with the coordination organ.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Operations organ.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can only confirm the part of this report that is based on my note that pertains to the three captured Serb soldiers, and the fact that the people in the El Mujahid Detachment did not allow the takeover of those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And does it also say in this paragraph -- does it also discuss 11 members of Bosniak-Muslims from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were those the soldiers that you referred to a few moments ago that you saw in the house?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but these were not soldiers. They were members of the so-called "Work Platoon." They were soldiers of the Republika Srpska Army who were there to provide support to the other troops to dig and set up shelters, dig trenches, bring water, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me on that. But were those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt? I'm sorry. Sir, this document talks, as Madam Sartorio said, it talks of 11 members of Bosniaks, Muslims from Prijedor, located in the 35th Division. But at the beginning of that paragraph, above there, it says: "Until 1.00, according to our checked information, the El Mudjahedin Detachment in the village of Livade had 11 Chetnik prisoners." Are you able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that more prisoners were brought in during that day and that they are referred to in this report. I cannot confirm that because I didn't see them. What I can say with certainty is that I saw the three Serb prisoners and the 11 Bosniaks from the Work Platoon. The other information was probably obtained from the operations organ, and this formed the basis for this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Sir, did you personally sign this report or was it signed by somebody else on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the signature, so I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the signature part be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry, I was -- I assumed that that was happening. Could we enlarge the bottom of the page that the witness has, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a signature at all? Is your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it either. Could we perhaps clarify that, Madam Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you explain to the Judges what is on the document? There appears to be a stamp. Could you explain how this document would be completed and how you would know that? And explain to the Judges what the stamp means.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: The stamp at the end of the document, at the bottom of the document, is the stamp confirming the receipt of this document on the part of the Military Security Service Department in the 3rd Corps, so this is the stamp containing the reference number under which this document is logged in at the 3rd Corps Security Department after its receipt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But, no, I think the specific question is: Why isn't this document signed or signed on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it was also sent via packet radio. You can see that at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And that being at the top of the document, is it that square, is that what that means, was sent --

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, to the left. It's on the left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And obviously can we zero in on both the English and the B/C/S left-hand corner. On the first page of the English document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So what is it exactly, sir, that tells you this was sent by packet communications?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He doesn't see the left of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: We have the information here for the processing of this document on the part of the operator who worked the packet communications system, and you have the date and the time when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with something else here. When we talk about the original, did you sign the original or was it signed by one of your associates? We see "for" written here. What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't confirm that unless I see the original with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So therefore, sir, is this a copy, not the original?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that this is a copy, since this was sent by packet communications. We understand the procedure. But at the bottom of the page on this copy, you can see whether this was signed by the person whose name is listed here or whether it was signed for that person. Does it say "for" here? And in the B/C/S version, I cannot see whether this word "for" can be seen. What I want to know, because I don't understand, is how the witness is unable to confirm the contents of his whole report if he signed it. I can understand that if somebody signed it on his behalf. That is why I want to clarify this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, when you -- this report, I think you said earlier, contains information that was obtained in your -- the security organ from other organs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So this report would contain your observations as well as observations, say, perhaps from the Intelligence Department?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this report was made by my associates on the basis of all that. And if I signed this report, that was a token of my trust in my associates, and I had no reason to doubt them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So if this document has your name on it, did you -- did you read it and did you understand what you were sending, and did you adopt what was in the document, because you are signing it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: One more quick question about this document. On page 2 of English -- sir, in the document there is a list of three names. Do you recall whether these were the three prisoners that you saw in that house in Livade on the 22nd of July?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. We would ask that this document be admitted in evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Isn't it already?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Sorry, sorry. Okay, thank you. I would like the witness now to be shown Exhibit 456, which is 2284 on the list that I sent Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to identify this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not draft this document, and I can't see the whole of it. But I assume that this is an operational report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown briefly the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Whose name is on that -- on the signature page, sir?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Fadil Hasanagic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then we'll go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, does this -- does this purport to be a report coming from the commander of the 31st Division, Hasanagic, to the 3rd Corps commander -- Command?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the 35th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The 35th to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that it is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you see a time that is indicated on the first page of this document, up in the -- on the left-hand side of the page?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the document that we just looked at, which was your document, would that have -- do you know if that was sent prior to 2130?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: The previous report, from what I could see, was sent at around 1600 hours, thereabouts, so it was earlier than this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I would like the witness to be -- page 2 of English for the Judges, and it starts at the bottom of page 1 in the Bosnian form. It begins with -- it's the large paragraph. It's about halfway down the paragraph: "After processing confiscated documents ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you see that section of your document, sir?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if we just go to the next paragraph: "After interrogating the imprisoned Chetniks ...," if you could just read that -- the next three sentences.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the part that speaks about the Muslim prisoners and members of the Republika Srpska Army who had come from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the English be turned to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, is this the same -- the content of what you just read, is this the same event that is a part of your report?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I assume so, because my report is just a part of this report. This report contains more information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But this is about the July 22nd discovery of the prisoners, is that fair to say, that this document also talks about that incident?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I assume so, because I didn't draft this document, so I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. I understand, sir. But in July of 1995, were there any other instances of prisoners being taken into custody that you recall?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We can put this document away, Your Honours, and I'd like the witness to be shown P02286.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, I know you didn't author this document either, but would you agree with me that the date is the same as the other two documents, the 22nd of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And does this document appear to be -- it's being sent from the 3rd Corps to the General Staff of the Army?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of page 1 in English -- well, excuse me. Before I get to that, the third paragraph down, which begins: "The Chetnik forces ...," if the Judges could be shown that, it talks about the 11 Muslims who were used as working detail. Is that the same incident that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't take part in any incidents, but I assume that these are the Bosniaks that are being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for correcting that. It wasn't probably completely accurate to call it being involved in an incident, but we're talking about the interviews -- your attempted interviews of the POWs on the 22nd of July. Okay. And if we go further down, there's a sentence that begins: "All captives are under control of the El Mudjahedin Detachment who did not allow access to them," and it discusses two doctors and one nurse among the captives. Sir, are these the three VRS soldiers that you tried to interview?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any women among the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you think there should have been women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it says here a nurse, a female nurse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a male nurse before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we have a different term for that, "medicinski tehnicar," male nurse.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, "medicinska sestra" is female nurse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the word in Bosnian denotes a female nurse. Over to you, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, just one more note on this document. On the second page of the English version, at the last sentence of the document before the signatures, sir, do you see that? It discusses the ARBiH 35th Division security organs. It mentions that they're engaged in collecting information. And that is your security organ; correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is the security organ of the 35th Division. The reference here is probably to the security organs across the battalions and brigades at the 35th Division. They continued to be active in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, I just want to understand the last answer given by the witness. If he says, "No, this is the security organ of the 35th Division," in which division were you? Were you not in the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you not in the security organ of that division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: Is this document -- wait a minute, let me read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I can help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, at line 24, I said: "Just one more note on this document. On the second page of the English version at the last sentence of the document before the signature, sir, do you see that, it discusses the ARBiH 35th Division security organs? It mentions that they're engaged in collecting information. Is that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that your security organ, and then you say, "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security organ of the 3rd Corps informs its superiors that the security organ of the 35th Division continues to work on gathering intelligence in the field. This is a report by the security organ of the 3rd Corps, or at least that's what they stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but the question was: Does that sentence refer to your security organ that is going to continue to collect information? And you said "no." Now, that organ that has been referred to is the 35th Division security organ to which I thought you belonged, so it should have been "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 580.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Your Honour, to speak with my senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. May the witness be shown P02300. And the Bosnian version at the bottom of the page so the witness can see, and on the second page for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, I know you didn't sign this document. Can you tell us whose name is there at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Alihodzic, Ekrem Alihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I believe you told us earlier that he was the assistant commander for the security organ of the 3rd Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I ask you to look at page 1 of the report, and page 1 in English as well. Oh, it's only one page in Bosnian. At the top, do you agree this document says it is going to the Army of RBiH, General Staff, Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if you look at the first paragraph and -- actually, if you read the entire document, which if you could read as much as you need to read, is this the incident of the July 22nd POWs that you saw? Is this the substance of this report?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was copied from the report by the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we request that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I just ask you about the fate of the two groups of prisoners. I understand from this and from the previous document that the 11 prisoners who were Bosniaks but who had served for the Republika Srpska Army, that they were originally detained by the El Mujahid Detachment, but subsequently released into the custody of the ABiH. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were surrendered to the BH Army military police and taken to Zenica. I do not know what became of them later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. While the three Serb POWs were kept by the El Mujahid Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And my question is, then: Do you know why this difference was made? Why were the 11 handed over to the military police, but the three Serbs were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, and I don't know who took that decision, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Took which decision? Sorry. Right, okay, so you mean the decision to keep them apart, to keep the two groups apart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we scroll down the English document, please. Thank you very much. Right down. Keep going. Go to the next page. Could you go to the next page, please. Okay, you can go back to the next page -- to the first page. I have a question. This document talks about the El Mudjahedin Detachment, in the combat activities, capturing 11 enemy soldiers. And then it says, in the third paragraph: "All the captured aggressor soldiers are members of the Light Prnjavor Brigade, and among them were ..." It mentions three. Where it starts talking about the 11 people, can this be explained, why the remaining eight are not mentioned or a separate eleven is not mentioned, particularly because that paragraph says "among them were." It doesn't say this is the total number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no explanation to offer. The 11 Muslims that were separated are referred to at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm getting no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I pressed the wrong button by mistake. Sorry. Okay, thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if anyone from your -- the security division -- the security organ of the 35th Division ever interviewed these prisoners that you -- that were encountered on the 22nd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I later left the area, and I didn't talk to anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know if they were ever interviewed by anyone else -- I mean anywhere else by anyone from your --

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You don't know or --

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I'd ask the document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Can I just see the heading of this document? Thank you, thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 582.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Unless I'm mistaken, there was that previous document which you say you signed. There is a reference in that document to the following: The fact that there was someone with you who was from the Intelligence Department. Do you remember that, sir, being referred to in that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
